newsitem.title: POLAND: French, German ministers reassure Poland over NATO.
newsitem.headline: French, German ministers reassure Poland over NATO.

text.p: A Polish official said on Monday his country had been reassured by the visiting defence ministers of Germany and France that it was firmly on track for NATO entry despite Russia's campaign against the move.
France's Charles Millon, Volker Ruehe of Germany and Stanislaw Dobrzanski held talks and the visitors also met Poland's Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz and President Aleksander Kwasniewski.

"We have recently witnessed complex Russian diplomatic activity, and therefore it was so important to get confirmation from the ministers that the process of expanding NATO will be continued and timetables will be kept," senior Kwasniewski aide Marek Siwiec told reporters.
The ministers were later due to sign an agreement on intensified military cooperation between their nations.

The three countries are linked in the Weimar Triangle, an understanding which straddles World War Two and Cold War divisions, and which Poland sees as a key to its rapid integration into the European Union and NATO.

Poland expects to be in the first group of countries, along with the Czech Republic and Hungary, to be invited to join NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organisation) at a summit of the Western defence alliance in Madrid next June.

The Weimar Triangle came into being with a 1991 meeting of the three countries' foreign ministers and has since grown to embrace military and other links as well. A summit of the three heads of state is planned for this year in Poland.

The Warsaw meeting coincided with a two-day visit to Warsaw by the chairman of Russia's parliament, Gennady Seleznyov, who reiterated Moscow's opposition to the eastward expansion of NATO, which it views as a threat.
On Monday Seleznyov was meeting Prime Minister Cimoszewicz and Polish parliamentarians.

Meanwhile on Monday foreign policy experts from the Polish opposition urged the government to adopt a clearer, firmer policy over recently-launched talks on a deal between NATO and Russia over the pact's expansion.

The Foreign Policy Council, grouping among others former foreign minister Krzysztof Skubiszewski and former defence minister Janusz Onyszkiewicz, said Poland should oppose giving Moscow special privileges in links with NATO, which the candidates to become new members of the pact would not enjoy.

"We cannot accept a situation in which Russia, a non-member of NATO, would have more participation and influence in various NATO institutions than countries, which...aspire to membership," Onyszkiewicz told a news conference.
He said Poland should demand that its voice be heard during Russia-NATO talks and that there should be no behind-the-scenes deal over expansion.
Russia's Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov is due to meet NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana on February 23 in Brussels.
